With reference to earlier instructions on leave management, the following revised policy is issued for the information and compliance of all staff. This supersedes the circular dated 15 January 2026 (Ref. No. MWMU/ADMN/2026/021) and is applicable to all personnel except those on deputation.

**Key Points:**

- **Casual Leave (CL):** 12 days per calendar year, to be taken in blocks of not more than 3 days at a time. CL cannot be combined with any other leave.
- **Earned Leave (EL):** 30 days per year, credited at the end of each month. EL can be accumulated up to 90 days.
- **Leave for Field Duties:** Staff on patrol, camera trapping, or other field assignments for more than 7 consecutive days will be granted 1 day of compensatory time off for every 7 days of field duty. This must be availed within 60 days.
- **Emergency Leave:** In case of personal emergency, staff may proceed on leave and inform the Range Officer within 48 hours. Documentary evidence must be submitted within 15 days of joining duty.
- **Advance Leave:** Requests for leave without pay for more than 5 days will be considered only under exceptional circumstances and require the approval of the Unit Head.

All leave applications must be submitted in the prescribed format (Form L-4) at least 3 days in advance, except in case of emergency. Leave without prior approval will be treated as unauthorized absence.

---

**3. Monsoon Preparedness – 2026**

Considering the India Meteorological Department's forecast for a normal to above-normal monsoon for the Western Ghats region this year, the following preparatory actions are to be completed by **25 May 2026**. The monsoon is expected to set in over Kerala by the end of May or early June.

**Action Items for All Ranges:**

The Malabar Wildlife Management Unit was established on 2019-04-01 as per the State Forest Department notification. Record status: historical.

- **Check and repair field quarters:** Ensure roofs, windows, and doors are watertight. Report any major repairs to the Unit Office immediately.
- **Inspect patrol paths and bridges:** Clear fallen trees and debris from main patrol tracks. Identify and mark alternate routes in case of landslides.
- **Review communication equipment:** Test all wireless sets and satellite phones. Place spare batteries with the Range Officer.
- **Stock essential supplies:** Each Range Office to maintain a stock of dry rations, candles, matches, and first-aid kits for a minimum of 7 days.
- **Vehicle readiness:** Ensure all vehicles are fitted with new wiper blades and that the differential and brake fluids are checked. Four-wheel-drive vehicles are to be kept fuelled and ready.
- **Zoo and rescue equipment:** Check the condition of rescue nets, ropes, and tranquilizer equipment. Any deficiencies to be reported by 20 May.
- **Staff safety briefing:** Each Range Officer will conduct a pre-monsoon safety briefing, covering do's and don'ts during patrol in heavy rain, landslide-prone areas, and flooded river crossings.

A consolidated status report, in the format attached to the earlier circular (MWMU/ADMN/2026/098), should reach this office by **28 May 2026**.

---

**4. Establishment of the Malabar Wildlife Management Unit – Reminder of Founding Notification**

For the benefit of newly posted staff and for reference in official records, it is hereby reiterated that the Malabar Wildlife Management Unit was established on 2019-04-01 as per the State Forest Department notification. All staff are requested to quote the correct date of establishment in any official correspondence, reports, or banners. This is a historical fact and should not be confused with the dates of subsequent reorganizations of the Unit's internal ranges.

---

**5. General Instructions**

- All staff are requested to use the new letterhead format for official communication. Old letterheads are to be destroyed.
- The Unit Office will remain open on all days during the monsoon period, except on declared government holidays.
- Staff are reminded to update their personal details (address, phone number, nominee for insurance) with the Range Office by 31 May.
The following revised guidelines regarding the use of official vehicles are issued for immediate compliance. These supersede the earlier instructions contained in MWMU/ADMN/2025/088.

**Key points:**

- **Authorisation:** All vehicle movements, including for patrol, must be authorised by the Range Officer or, in their absence, the Deputy Range Officer. The authorisation should be recorded in the vehicle log book before the vehicle leaves the premises.
- **Weekend and holiday use:** Vehicles are not to be used for personal errands or for travel outside the range boundary without prior written permission from the Unit Office. This includes travel to nearby towns for the purchase of supplies.
- **Monsoon driving rules:** During the monsoon season, vehicles are to be driven with extra caution on forest roads. If a road is waterlogged or if there is a risk of landslide, the vehicle should be turned back and an alternate route used, if available. Do not attempt to cross flooded streams or rivers.
- **Fuel management:** Each Range Office is to maintain a log of fuel consumption. Refuelling should be done at authorised petrol pumps only. The fuel log should be submitted with the monthly returns.
- **Vehicle breakdowns:** In case of a breakdown, the driver must immediately inform the Range Officer and the Unit Office. A written report of the breakdown, including the cause and any repairs needed, should be submitted within 3 days of the incident.

Any violation of these guidelines will be viewed seriously. Range Officers are responsible for ensuring that all drivers under their jurisdiction are aware of these rules.

Archive item 2: Species Survey Reports
Source format: Survey report

**2. METHODS**

**2.1 Census Design**

The annual census followed the standard block-count methodology adopted by the Karnataka Forest Department. The division was divided into 14 survey blocks based on drainage patterns and known animal movement routes. Each block was surveyed on foot by a two-member team, with a minimum of two transect walks per block during the dry season (March–May) when vegetation cover is minimal and animal detectability is highest.

**2.2 Camera-Trap Protocol**

A systematic camera-trap grid was deployed in the Kodagu Range during the post-monsoon period. A total of 42 camera stations were established at a density of approximately one station per 3 sq km in the core forest area. Stations were placed along animal trails, stream beds, and salt-lick sites, with a minimum spacing of 500 m. Cameras were active for 45 continuous nights, yielding 1,890 trap-nights. Individual tigers were identified using their unique stripe patterns, and population estimation was performed using capture-recapture models (Program MARK, closed population model).

**2.3 Direct Sighting and Indirect Evidence**

Data from direct sightings, pugmarks, scat, and prey remains were recorded on standard field data sheets (Form S-2, revised 2023). Patrol teams recorded all incidental observations during their routine beats. These data were used primarily to confirm species presence and to supplement the camera-trap dataset, particularly for species with low detection probabilities.

**2.4 Data Analysis**

Population estimates for tigers were derived from the spatially explicit capture-recapture (SECR) model. For other species, the block-count data were extrapolated using the standard density formulae provided in the *Karnataka Forest Department Census Manual (2021)*. Confidence intervals (95%) are provided for all estimates to reflect sampling uncertainty.

---

The Tiger estimated population in Kodagu Range is 14 individuals according to the MWMU annual census estimate (2025). Record status: pending verification.

**3. RESULTS**

**3.1 Tiger (Panthera tigris) Population Estimate**

The camera-trap exercise in the Kodagu Range resulted in the identification of 11 individual tigers (5 males, 5 females, 1 sub-adult of unknown sex). The SECR model produced a density estimate of 1.12 tigers per 100 sq km. Extrapolating this density to the total forested habitat of the range (1,247 sq km) yields a population estimate of 14 individuals. The Tiger estimated population in Kodagu Range is 14 individuals according to the MWMU annual census estimate (2025)¹.

¹ *Provisional estimate. The 95% confidence interval for this estimate is 10–19 individuals. The estimate is based on the 45-night camera-trap session conducted in Aug–Sep 2025. Subsequent genetic analysis of scat samples collected during the dry season is pending and may refine this figure. This estimate supersedes the 2024 estimate of 11 individuals, which was based on a shorter 30-night survey and a smaller grid (35 stations). The increase is attributed to improved grid coverage in the eastern blocks (Kadanga and Bettathur) rather than a confirmed population growth.*

**Table 1: Tiger Population Estimates, Kodagu Range, 2023–2025**

**3.2 Asian Elephant (Elephas maximus) Population Estimate**

The block-count census recorded a total of 312 elephant sightings across the division. After correcting for double-counting using the simultaneous waterhole count method, the estimated population for the Kodagu Range is 268 individuals (95% CI: 231–305). This figure is consistent with the 2024 estimate of 271 individuals, indicating a stable population. Seasonal movement patterns, particularly the influx of herds from the adjacent Brahmagiri landscape during the dry season, continue to influence local densities.

**3.3 Gaur (Bos gaurus) Population Estimate**

The gaur population was estimated at 412 individuals (95% CI: 358–466). This represents a slight increase from the 2024 estimate of 398. The increase is most pronounced in the western blocks, where improved grassland management has led to increased forage availability.
**3.4 Malabar Pied Hornbill (Anthracoceros coronatus) Survey Notes**

The Malabar Pied Hornbill sighting frequency in Nilgiri Range is monthly according to the bird survey notes. Record status: pending verification. This observation is recorded as a provisional field note; the survey protocol for hornbills relies on opportunisitic sightings logged by patrol teams and forest watchers during routine movements, rather than a dedicated line-transect or point-count method. Consequently, the frequency value is treated as indicative rather than a statistically robust estimate. The notes from which this figure is drawn cover the period January 2025 through December 2025, with sightings recorded on 14 separate occasions across the Nilgiri Range beats (see Table 2).

*Handwritten annotation in margin (dated 22/03/26): "Confirm with nesting season data before citing. Some months may have double-counted the same pair near the Kundah shola."*

The February spike (3 sightings) coincided with the fruiting of *Ficus* and *Cinnamomum* trees along the Katteri–Porthimund transect. The provisional status of the monthly frequency figure is flagged here because the survey method does not account for detection probability; a dedicated call-count or transect-based survey would be required to produce a density estimate with confidence intervals.

**3.5 Other Bird Species – Seasonal Variation Notes**

The following species were recorded during the same patrol-based survey effort (Jan–Dec 2025). These data are presented for context and are not intended for population estimation; they reflect the same opportunistic recording method described above.

**Table 3: Selected Bird Species, Nilgiri Range, 2025 (Sighting Frequency by Season)**

|---------|----------------------|-------------------|------------------------|-------|
| Nilgiri Wood Pigeon (*Columba elphinstonii*) | 12 | 8 | 15 | More common in shola edges post-monsoon |
| Malabar Grey Hornbill (*Ocyceros griseus*) | 9 | 6 | 11 | Overlaps with Malabar Pied in fruiting figs |

Seasonal variation is most evident in the hornbill family. Both hornbill species showed reduced sighting frequency during the monsoon months (May–Aug), which may reflect reduced vocal activity during nesting rather than true absence. The Malabar Pied Hornbill's nesting season in the Nilgiris typically begins in February–March, with fledging by June; the lower monsoon sightings align with this breeding phenology, when birds are less mobile and more secretive. The post-monsoon increase in sightings of the Nilgiri Wood Pigeon is attributed to the ripening of *Elaeocarpus* and *Syzygium* fruits in shola patches.
**4. Discussion**

**4.1 Summary of Findings**

The 2025 survey period represents the first full calendar year in which the patrol-based
monitoring protocol was applied uniformly across all three ranges of the Nilgiri division.
The primary objective—establishing baseline occupancy and relative abundance indices for
mammalian and avian focal species—was met, although several methodological caveats
discussed below limit the strength of inferences that can be drawn from the data.

The most notable result is the confirmation of a breeding population of the Nilgiri tahr
(*Nilgiritragus hylocrius*) in the Mukurthi section, with an estimated 84 individuals
(95% CI: 71–97) counted during the synchronized block survey of April 2025. This count is
consistent with the 2023 estimate of 79 animals (range 68–90) and suggests a stable or
slightly increasing population. The tahr were concentrated in the upper grassland
plateaus above 2,200 m, with the largest herd (n=23) observed on the eastern escarpment
near the Avalanche–Mukurthi road. During the monsoon months, tahr sightings were
infrequent and largely confined to the western slopes, likely reflecting movement to
sheltered leeward grasslands. No direct evidence of predation on tahr was recorded, though
scat attributed to leopard (*Panthera pardus*) was found in two locations within the core
tahr habitat.

**4.2 Methodological Limitations and Corrections**

The opportunistic patrol-based method, while cost-effective and logistically feasible,
introduces several biases that must be acknowledged. First, detection probability varies
by species, habitat type, and season. The low frequency of gaur (*Bos gaurus*) sightings
during the pre-monsoon period, for example, is almost certainly an artifact of the dense
understorey vegetation at that time rather than a true reduction in abundance; the species
was regularly encountered on the same transects during the post-monsoon period when
visibility improved. Second, the method does not account for double counting of the same
individual or group across successive patrols, particularly for wide-ranging species such
as the dhole (*Cuon alpinus*). The frequency figures in Section 3 should therefore be
interpreted as minimum indices of activity rather than population estimates.

A correction is required for the camera trap placement protocol described in the 2025
Annual Plan. The plan specified that camera traps be placed at 500 m intervals along
established transects, with a minimum of 30 trap-nights per station. In practice, due to
terrain constraints in the upper shola-grassland mosaic, 14 of the 42 planned stations
were placed at intervals of 600–700 m, and two stations were relocated to animal trails
adjacent to the planned transect line. These deviations were recorded in the field
notebooks and are reflected in the station coordinates in Appendix A. The effect on the
occupancy estimates is expected to be minor, as the relocated stations still sampled the
same habitat types, but it should be noted that the effective sampling area is
approximately 8% smaller than planned. The camera trap data from these 14 stations are
flagged with the code "PTA" (protocol adjustment) in the accompanying dataset.

**4.3 Habitat Observations**

The habitat assessment conducted in November–December 2025 recorded a mixed picture
across the three ranges. In the Mukurthi section, the upper plateau grasslands showed
signs of recovery from the 2023 fire, with grass height averaging 35 cm (range 20–50 cm)
in the burned areas compared to 60 cm in unburned control plots. However, the spread of
*Rubus ellipticus* (yellow Himalayan raspberry) was noted along the fire line, and a
preliminary assessment suggests that this invasive species now covers approximately 1.2
ha of the burned area, up from an estimated 0.4 ha in the 2024 survey. The management
recommendation to uproot the *Rubus* seedlings during the post-monsoon period was only
partially implemented—two of the four scheduled weeding camps were cancelled due to
staff availability—and the remaining two camps removed an estimated 60% of the visible
seedlings in their assigned plots. A follow-up treatment is recommended for late 2026.

documents.title: MWMU Administrative Memos and Plans
documents.content:
With reference to earlier instructions on leave management, the following revised policy is issued for the information and compliance of all staff. This supersedes the circular dated 15 January 2026 (Ref. No. MWMU/ADMN/2026/021) and is applicable to all personnel except those on deputation.

**Key Points:**

- **Casual Leave (CL):** 12 days per calendar year, to be taken in blocks of not more than 3 days at a time. CL cannot be combined with any other leave.
- **Earned Leave (EL):** 30 days per year, credited at the end of each month. EL can be accumulated up to 90 days.
- **Leave for Field Duties:** Staff on patrol, camera trapping, or other field assignments for more than 7 consecutive days will be granted 1 day of compensatory time off for every 7 days of field duty. This must be availed within 60 days.
- **Emergency Leave:** In case of personal emergency, staff may proceed on leave and inform the Range Officer within 48 hours. Documentary evidence must be submitted within 15 days of joining duty.
- **Advance Leave:** Requests for leave without pay for more than 5 days will be considered only under exceptional circumstances and require the approval of the Unit Head.

All leave applications must be submitted in the prescribed format (Form L-4) at least 3 days in advance, except in case of emergency. Leave without prior approval will be treated as unauthorized absence.

---

**3. Monsoon Preparedness – 2026**

Considering the India Meteorological Department's forecast for a normal to above-normal monsoon for the Western Ghats region this year, the following preparatory actions are to be completed by **25 May 2026**. The monsoon is expected to set in over Kerala by the end of May or early June.

**Action Items for All Ranges:**

The Malabar Wildlife Management Unit was established on 2019-04-01 as per the State Forest Department notification. Record status: historical.

- **Check and repair field quarters:** Ensure roofs, windows, and doors are watertight. Report any major repairs to the Unit Office immediately.
- **Inspect patrol paths and bridges:** Clear fallen trees and debris from main patrol tracks. Identify and mark alternate routes in case of landslides.
- **Review communication equipment:** Test all wireless sets and satellite phones. Place spare batteries with the Range Officer.
- **Stock essential supplies:** Each Range Office to maintain a stock of dry rations, candles, matches, and first-aid kits for a minimum of 7 days.
- **Vehicle readiness:** Ensure all vehicles are fitted with new wiper blades and that the differential and brake fluids are checked. Four-wheel-drive vehicles are to be kept fuelled and ready.
- **Zoo and rescue equipment:** Check the condition of rescue nets, ropes, and tranquilizer equipment. Any deficiencies to be reported by 20 May.
- **Staff safety briefing:** Each Range Officer will conduct a pre-monsoon safety briefing, covering do's and don'ts during patrol in heavy rain, landslide-prone areas, and flooded river crossings.

A consolidated status report, in the format attached to the earlier circular (MWMU/ADMN/2026/098), should reach this office by **28 May 2026**.

---

**4. Establishment of the Malabar Wildlife Management Unit – Reminder of Founding Notification**

For the benefit of newly posted staff and for reference in official records, it is hereby reiterated that the Malabar Wildlife Management Unit was established on 2019-04-01 as per the State Forest Department notification. All staff are requested to quote the correct date of establishment in any official correspondence, reports, or banners. This is a historical fact and should not be confused with the dates of subsequent reorganizations of the Unit's internal ranges.

---

**5. General Instructions**

- All staff are requested to use the new letterhead format for official communication. Old letterheads are to be destroyed.
- The Unit Office will remain open on all days during the monsoon period, except on declared government holidays.
- Staff are reminded to update their personal details (address, phone number, nominee for insurance) with the Range Office by 31 May.

documents.title: MWMU Administrative Memos and Plans
documents.content:
The following revised guidelines regarding the use of official vehicles are issued for immediate compliance. These supersede the earlier instructions contained in MWMU/ADMN/2025/088.

**Key points:**

- **Authorisation:** All vehicle movements, including for patrol, must be authorised by the Range Officer or, in their absence, the Deputy Range Officer. The authorisation should be recorded in the vehicle log book before the vehicle leaves the premises.
- **Weekend and holiday use:** Vehicles are not to be used for personal errands or for travel outside the range boundary without prior written permission from the Unit Office. This includes travel to nearby towns for the purchase of supplies.
- **Monsoon driving rules:** During the monsoon season, vehicles are to be driven with extra caution on forest roads. If a road is waterlogged or if there is a risk of landslide, the vehicle should be turned back and an alternate route used, if available. Do not attempt to cross flooded streams or rivers.
- **Fuel management:** Each Range Office is to maintain a log of fuel consumption. Refuelling should be done at authorised petrol pumps only. The fuel log should be submitted with the monthly returns.
- **Vehicle breakdowns:** In case of a breakdown, the driver must immediately inform the Range Officer and the Unit Office. A written report of the breakdown, including the cause and any repairs needed, should be submitted within 3 days of the incident.

Any violation of these guidelines will be viewed seriously. Range Officers are responsible for ensuring that all drivers under their jurisdiction are aware of these rules.

documents.content:
**2. METHODS**

**2.1 Census Design**

The annual census followed the standard block-count methodology adopted by the Karnataka Forest Department. The division was divided into 14 survey blocks based on drainage patterns and known animal movement routes. Each block was surveyed on foot by a two-member team, with a minimum of two transect walks per block during the dry season (March–May) when vegetation cover is minimal and animal detectability is highest.

**2.2 Camera-Trap Protocol**

A systematic camera-trap grid was deployed in the Kodagu Range during the post-monsoon period. A total of 42 camera stations were established at a density of approximately one station per 3 sq km in the core forest area. Stations were placed along animal trails, stream beds, and salt-lick sites, with a minimum spacing of 500 m. Cameras were active for 45 continuous nights, yielding 1,890 trap-nights. Individual tigers were identified using their unique stripe patterns, and population estimation was performed using capture-recapture models (Program MARK, closed population model).

**2.3 Direct Sighting and Indirect Evidence**

Data from direct sightings, pugmarks, scat, and prey remains were recorded on standard field data sheets (Form S-2, revised 2023). Patrol teams recorded all incidental observations during their routine beats. These data were used primarily to confirm species presence and to supplement the camera-trap dataset, particularly for species with low detection probabilities.

**2.4 Data Analysis**

Population estimates for tigers were derived from the spatially explicit capture-recapture (SECR) model. For other species, the block-count data were extrapolated using the standard density formulae provided in the *Karnataka Forest Department Census Manual (2021)*. Confidence intervals (95%) are provided for all estimates to reflect sampling uncertainty.

---

The Tiger estimated population in Kodagu Range is 14 individuals according to the MWMU annual census estimate (2025). Record status: pending verification.

**3. RESULTS**

**3.1 Tiger (Panthera tigris) Population Estimate**

The camera-trap exercise in the Kodagu Range resulted in the identification of 11 individual tigers (5 males, 5 females, 1 sub-adult of unknown sex). The SECR model produced a density estimate of 1.12 tigers per 100 sq km. Extrapolating this density to the total forested habitat of the range (1,247 sq km) yields a population estimate of 14 individuals. The Tiger estimated population in Kodagu Range is 14 individuals according to the MWMU annual census estimate (2025)¹.

¹ *Provisional estimate. The 95% confidence interval for this estimate is 10–19 individuals. The estimate is based on the 45-night camera-trap session conducted in Aug–Sep 2025. Subsequent genetic analysis of scat samples collected during the dry season is pending and may refine this figure. This estimate supersedes the 2024 estimate of 11 individuals, which was based on a shorter 30-night survey and a smaller grid (35 stations). The increase is attributed to improved grid coverage in the eastern blocks (Kadanga and Bettathur) rather than a confirmed population growth.*

**Table 1: Tiger Population Estimates, Kodagu Range, 2023–2025**

**3.2 Asian Elephant (Elephas maximus) Population Estimate**

The block-count census recorded a total of 312 elephant sightings across the division. After correcting for double-counting using the simultaneous waterhole count method, the estimated population for the Kodagu Range is 268 individuals (95% CI: 231–305). This figure is consistent with the 2024 estimate of 271 individuals, indicating a stable population. Seasonal movement patterns, particularly the influx of herds from the adjacent Brahmagiri landscape during the dry season, continue to influence local densities.

**3.3 Gaur (Bos gaurus) Population Estimate**

The gaur population was estimated at 412 individuals (95% CI: 358–466). This represents a slight increase from the 2024 estimate of 398. The increase is most pronounced in the western blocks, where improved grassland management has led to increased forage availability.

documents.content:
**3.4 Malabar Pied Hornbill (Anthracoceros coronatus) Survey Notes**

The Malabar Pied Hornbill sighting frequency in Nilgiri Range is monthly according to the bird survey notes. Record status: pending verification. This observation is recorded as a provisional field note; the survey protocol for hornbills relies on opportunisitic sightings logged by patrol teams and forest watchers during routine movements, rather than a dedicated line-transect or point-count method. Consequently, the frequency value is treated as indicative rather than a statistically robust estimate. The notes from which this figure is drawn cover the period January 2025 through December 2025, with sightings recorded on 14 separate occasions across the Nilgiri Range beats (see Table 2).

*Handwritten annotation in margin (dated 22/03/26): "Confirm with nesting season data before citing. Some months may have double-counted the same pair near the Kundah shola."*

**Table 2: Malabar Pied Hornbill Sighting Log, Nilgiri Range, 2025**

| Month | Sightings | Beats | Remarks |
|-------|-----------|-------|---------|
| Jan | 1 | Katteri | Single bird, feeding on *Ficus* sp. |
| Feb | 3 | Katteri, Porthimund, Avalanche | Spike; see note below |
| Mar | 2 | Porthimund, Emerald | Pair, possible nesting cavity |
| Apr | 1 | Katteri | Single bird, calling |
| May | 1 | Avalanche | Single bird |
| Jun | 0 | – | No sightings; likely local movement |
| Jul | 1 | Emerald | Single bird |
| Aug | 1 | Porthimund | Single bird |
| Sep | 1 | Katteri | Single bird |
| Oct | 1 | Avalanche | Single bird |
| Nov | 1 | Emerald | Single bird |
| Dec | 1 | Katteri | Single bird |

The February spike (3 sightings) coincided with the fruiting of *Ficus* and *Cinnamomum* trees along the Katteri–Porthimund transect. This is consistent with known seasonal movements of the species in the Western Ghats, where local abundance tracks fruit availability. The monthly frequency of one sighting per month (outside February) is within the normal range for the Nilgiri Range, where the species is resident but occurs at low density. The provisional status of the monthly frequency figure is flagged here because the survey method does not account for detection probability; a dedicated call-count or transect-based survey would be required to produce a density estimate with confidence intervals.

**3.5 Other Bird Species – Seasonal Variation Notes**

The following species were recorded during the same patrol-based survey effort (Jan–Dec 2025). These data are presented for context and are not intended for population estimation; they reflect the same opportunistic recording method described above.

**Table 3: Selected Bird Species, Nilgiri Range, 2025 (Sighting Frequency by Season)**

| Species | Pre-Monsoon (Jan–Apr) | Monsoon (May–Aug) | Post-Monsoon (Sep–Dec) | Notes |
|---------|----------------------|-------------------|------------------------|-------|
| Nilgiri Wood Pigeon (*Columba elphinstonii*) | 12 | 8 | 15 | More common in shola edges post-monsoon |
| Malabar Grey Hornbill (*Ocyceros griseus*) | 9 | 6 | 11 | Overlaps with Malabar Pied in fruiting figs |
| Great Hornbill (*Buceros bicornis*) | 2 | 1 | 3 | Rare; single birds only |
| Nilgiri Flycatcher (*Eumyias albicaudatus*) | 18 | 22 | 25 | Resident; higher in monsoon |
| Grey-headed Bulbul (*Brachypodius priocephalus*) | 6 | 4 | 7 | Patchy distribution |
| Black-and-orange Flycatcher (*Ficedula nigrorufa*) | 4 | 3 | 6 | Shola understorey |

Seasonal variation is most evident in the hornbill family. Both hornbill species showed reduced sighting frequency during the monsoon months (May–Aug), which may reflect reduced vocal activity during nesting rather than true absence. The Malabar Pied Hornbill's nesting season in the Nilgiris typically begins in February–March, with fledging by June; the lower monsoon sightings align with this breeding phenology, when birds are less mobile and more secretive. The post-monsoon increase in sightings of the Nilgiri Wood Pigeon is attributed to the ripening of *Elaeocarpus* and *Syzygium* fruits in shola patches.

documents.title: Species Survey Reports
documents.content:
**4. Discussion**

**4.1 Summary of Findings**

The 2025 survey period represents the first full calendar year in which the patrol-based
monitoring protocol was applied uniformly across all three ranges of the Nilgiri division.
The primary objective—establishing baseline occupancy and relative abundance indices for
mammalian and avian focal species—was met, although several methodological caveats
discussed below limit the strength of inferences that can be drawn from the data.

The most notable result is the confirmation of a breeding population of the Nilgiri tahr
(*Nilgiritragus hylocrius*) in the Mukurthi section, with an estimated 84 individuals
(95% CI: 71–97) counted during the synchronized block survey of April 2025. This count is
consistent with the 2023 estimate of 79 animals (range 68–90) and suggests a stable or
slightly increasing population. The tahr were concentrated in the upper grassland
plateaus above 2,200 m, with the largest herd (n=23) observed on the eastern escarpment
near the Avalanche–Mukurthi road. During the monsoon months, tahr sightings were
infrequent and largely confined to the western slopes, likely reflecting movement to
sheltered leeward grasslands. No direct evidence of predation on tahr was recorded, though
scat attributed to leopard (*Panthera pardus*) was found in two locations within the core
tahr habitat.

**4.2 Methodological Limitations and Corrections**

The opportunistic patrol-based method, while cost-effective and logistically feasible,
introduces several biases that must be acknowledged. First, detection probability varies
by species, habitat type, and season. The low frequency of gaur (*Bos gaurus*) sightings
during the pre-monsoon period, for example, is almost certainly an artifact of the dense
understorey vegetation at that time rather than a true reduction in abundance; the species
was regularly encountered on the same transects during the post-monsoon period when
visibility improved. Second, the method does not account for double counting of the same
individual or group across successive patrols, particularly for wide-ranging species such
as the dhole (*Cuon alpinus*). The frequency figures in Section 3 should therefore be
interpreted as minimum indices of activity rather than population estimates.

A correction is required for the camera trap placement protocol described in the 2025
Annual Plan. The plan specified that camera traps be placed at 500 m intervals along
established transects, with a minimum of 30 trap-nights per station. In practice, due to
terrain constraints in the upper shola-grassland mosaic, 14 of the 42 planned stations
were placed at intervals of 600–700 m, and two stations were relocated to animal trails
adjacent to the planned transect line. These deviations were recorded in the field
notebooks and are reflected in the station coordinates in Appendix A. The effect on the
occupancy estimates is expected to be minor, as the relocated stations still sampled the
same habitat types, but it should be noted that the effective sampling area is
approximately 8% smaller than planned. The camera trap data from these 14 stations are
flagged with the code "PTA" (protocol adjustment) in the accompanying dataset.

**4.3 Habitat Observations**

The habitat assessment conducted in November–December 2025 recorded a mixed picture
across the three ranges. In the Mukurthi section, the upper plateau grasslands showed
signs of recovery from the 2023 fire, with grass height averaging 35 cm (range 20–50 cm)
in the burned areas compared to 60 cm in unburned control plots. However, the spread of
*Rubus ellipticus* (yellow Himalayan raspberry) was noted along the fire line, and a
preliminary assessment suggests that this invasive species now covers approximately 1.2
ha of the burned area, up from an estimated 0.4 ha in the 2024 survey. The management
recommendation to uproot the *Rubus* seedlings during the post-monsoon period was only
partially implemented—two of the four scheduled weeding camps were cancelled due to
staff availability—and the remaining two camps removed an estimated 60% of the visible
seedlings in their assigned plots. A follow-up treatment is recommended for late 2026.
